statement: FIFO and pro-rata allocation produce different inventory and adverse-selection exposure under identical public flow and displayed depth.
representation_change: Treat matching allocation as a venue-level experimental factor with explicit rounding and residual rules.
causal_mechanism: Equal-price queue allocation determines which liquidity provider receives toxic and neutral flow, changing inventory and marked wealth.
assumptions: Allocation rules are implemented exactly and agents observe only public feed plus private fills.
predicted_observable: Different fill concentration and inventory-tail distributions at equal aggregate depth.
predicted_direction_or_delta: Unknown sign; not an optimization claim.
cheap_test: Two-maker, one-price-level deterministic allocation and conservation test.
falsifier: Difference disappears after fixing a queue, rounding, or event-order defect.

statement: A public triangular mispricing produces an economic effect only when all three delayed legs have executable depth, fees, and residual exposure accounted.
representation_change: Model an asset graph and a per-leg execution ledger rather than a midpoint parity signal.
causal_mechanism: Cross-pair trades couple liquidity and capital constraints; non-atomic fills turn nominal parity into residual risk.
assumptions: Every settlement denomination has an explicit valuation path.
predicted_observable: All-in cycle edge and terminal wealth differ from midpoint edge; failed legs leave recorded inventory.
predicted_direction_or_delta: Midpoint-only opportunities are rejected more often than they complete.
cheap_test: One deterministic three-book FOK/null scenario with a latency-label swap.
falsifier: Positive result persists after removing executable depth or omits a residual/fee.

statement: Inventory-aware A-S-style controls can reduce inventory tails without reducing useful displayed liquidity or cost-adjusted marked wealth.
representation_change: Evaluate a market maker as an organism with balance sheet, quote survival, fills, markouts, and terminal marked account, not quote counts.
causal_mechanism: Reservation-price skew moves quotes against inventory while volatility/fill-distance spread control prices inventory risk.
assumptions: Observed fill hazard by offset is a usable calibration diagnostic.
predicted_observable: Lower tail inventory conditional on comparable two-sided depth and fill opportunity.
cheap_test: One instrument, same noise path, linear-skew versus A-S maker control.
falsifier: Inventory reduction is entirely caused by cancelled/withdrawn quotes or no valid wealth benefit.

statement: A strategy's risk-normalized marked-equity-share growth depends on opponent composition and can exhibit a stable directed non-transitive cycle.
representation_change: Replace a global strategy ranking with a held-out directed invasion matrix over population mixtures.
causal_mechanism: Liquidity provision, arbitrage, and directional/derivative flow alter each other's available rents, inventory risk, and costs.
assumptions: Capital, risk limits, fees, and reporting numeraire are controlled across candidate populations.
predicted_observable: Significant directional invasion advantages that survive seed/label/order/mixture perturbations.
predicted_direction_or_delta: Unknown; a flat or transitive matrix is an equally valid result.
cheap_test: Two-strategy leave-one-out invasion matrix on a one-asset world.
falsifier: Advantages vanish or reverse on held-out mixtures, or arise from invalid terminal valuation.

statement: An explicit zero option-buy probability must remain zero rather than being conflated with an omitted baseline configuration.
representation_change: Represent optional treatment parameters with presence rather than zero-value sentinel semantics.
causal_mechanism: A zero-value default silently changes the directional-flow treatment, invalidating any gamma-sign or ecology comparison.
assumptions: JSON configuration distinguishes omitted fields from explicit numeric zero through nullable decoding.
predicted_observable: An explicit zero reaches option takers unchanged and omission retains the historical default.
cheap_test: Decode explicit zero and omitted JSON configurations, construct the simulation, and inspect normalized configuration.
falsifier: Explicit zero becomes a nonzero default or omitted configuration changes baseline behavior.

statement: Venue-local matching-rule configuration can select exact existing FIFO or pro-rata algorithms without changing causality outside a named venue.
representation_change: Attach allocation policy to venue identity rather than to an exchange-wide simulation flag.
causal_mechanism: Separate venue allocation rules create distinct equal-price fill incentives while deterministic ingress retains a fixed causal order.
assumptions: The existing matchers are exact for their documented simplified policies.
predicted_observable: A manifest maps each venue to its matcher type; unknown policy or venue fails construction.
cheap_test: Construct north FIFO, central/south pro-rata and inspect concrete matchers; reject invalid rules.
falsifier: Default policy changes, an unknown rule is accepted, or policy map iteration affects construction.
known_failure_modes: Mislabeling basic pro-rata as a real exchange hybrid

statement: A fitness experiment is valid only if every independently funded participant has explicit initial and terminal USD marked accounts.
representation_change: Promote participant identity and marked account rows to controller-owned first-class telemetry.
causal_mechanism: A single dealer account or router cashflow cannot rank an ecology; missing marks must invalidate rather than selectively omit participants.
assumptions: The current control world holds only USD/ABC balances and declares a bootstrap initial mark plus a terminal two-sided ABC/USD mark.
predicted_observable: Strict runs produce one initial and terminal row per participant with role/venue/client identity; an unpriceable terminal book fails.
cheap_test: Three-venue strict active control plus missing-mark and GOMAX invariance regressions.
falsifier: Any connected account is absent, lacks a USD report asset, terminal valuation uses a fallback last trade, or the rows differ across GOMAX settings.
known_failure_modes: Cross-currency asset graph not yet supported
initial bootstrap mark is not an executable mid

statement: A strict USD population report remains complete when every venue adds the minimal three-asset spot graph ABC/USD, CDF/USD, and ABC/CDF.
representation_change: Treat direct conversion books and their terminal two-sided marks as mandatory report inputs rather than inferring a cross rate or ignoring CDF balances.
causal_mechanism: Any participant that trades ABC/CDF acquires CDF exposure; its wealth is undefined in USD without an explicit CDF/USD conversion, so the run must fail when that mark is absent.
assumptions: ABC/USD and CDF/USD are independently quoted on every venue.
Gen-0 reports USD marked wealth but does not yet route a triangular arbitrage strategy.
predicted_observable: All participants have complete initial and terminal USD accounts, terminal provenance names both USD conversion marks, and those rows are identical at GOMAXPROCS 1 and 14.
cheap_test: Three-venue five-minute graph control plus strict account digest across GOMAXPROCS.
falsifier: Any CDF balance is omitted, terminal CDF/USD is one-sided/unavailable without failing the run, or account rows differ by GOMAXPROCS.
known_failure_modes: Triangle actor would treat midpoint parity as executable
cross-asset strategy could leak engine state
per-venue CDF quote withdrawal can invalidate a strict terminal mark

statement: A triangular signal is admissible only when coherent public top-of-book quotes support sequential bounded limit-FOK legs, quote-asset fees are included, and the observed fill ledger reports every residual.
representation_change: Replace simultaneous intent legs with a group ledger whose next limit-FOK amount is derived from actual prior fills and whose expected and observed USD/ABC/CDF deltas are explicit.
causal_mechanism: FOK prevents partial fill only within one book, not across instruments. Sequentially deriving the next leg from the previous fill avoids inventing inventory, while any reject terminates the group with explicit residual risk rather than claimed arbitrage PnL.
assumptions: The actor knows only its configured quote-fee schedule and delayed public feed.
Each leg is constrained to coherent observed best-level displayed quantity.
The initial control permits only known quote-denominated percentage fees.
A bounded CDF/USD limit-FOK unwind may remove declared rounding dust; otherwise the residual remains reported.
predicted_observable: Midpoint-only, stale, or under-depth cycles submit zero groups; an all-in positive cycle advances one observed fill at a time; a leg rejection submits no later leg and records actual USD/ABC/CDF deltas.
cheap_test: Direct actor fixtures for both directions, fees, stale timestamps, displayed depth, fill-derived sizing, one-leg rejection, and rounding dust.
falsifier: A group is submitted from a midpoint-only/stale/under-depth view, derives a later leg from intent instead of fill, reports completed with nonzero residual outside its bound, omits a fee, or treats rejected legs as zero-risk success.
known_failure_modes: foreign/base/fixed fees require a later fragmentation-aware admission contract
same-timestamp public snapshots can be causally ordered by the runtime

statement: A cross-quoted maker must calculate price, tick, and inventory risk in its contract quote units; a USD-parameterized ABC/CDF controller is not evidence about a CDF-quoted market.
representation_change: Use ABC/CDF quote precision 1e8 and convert the frozen-CDF baseline variance from USD^2/s to CDF^2/s before constructing its Stoikov controller.
causal_mechanism: A quote precision mismatch rescales the control input and makes spread/inventory response unrelated to the listed contract's monetary unit.
assumptions: The first revalidation uses a frozen CDF/USD bootstrap price solely to express the existing USD variance in CDF units.
predicted_observable: The corrected bootstrap controller returns finite positive two-sided ABC/CDF quotes and a five-minute strict graph control remains complete and deterministic.
cheap_test: Construct every cross-pair maker, assert CDF quote precision, converted variance, and a positive bootstrap quote; then repeat E-040 as a new run.
falsifier: The corrected controller has invalid bootstrap quotes, incomplete terminal valuation, or differs across host parallelism.
known_failure_modes: Frozen-CDF conversion is a synthetic control, not dynamic FX volatility
existing E-040 cannot be reused as economic evidence

claim: Spot market orders cannot use enabled spot margin, so any participant holding no inventory in the sold asset is silently unable to hedge or trade via market orders.
mechanism: checkMarketOrderFunds compared free balance directly and never reached tryReserveOrBorrow, which is the only auto-borrow entry point; limit orders therefore financed identical trades that market orders rejected.
falsifier: A spot market sell financed only by permitted borrowing is accepted before the fix, or an unfundable one is accepted after it.
impact: Every multivenue hedged-dealer arm using a zero-base endowment was in fact unhedged; hedge-on/off treatment contrast in such configs is invalid.

claim: The ABC/CDF Stoikov makers place an initial quote pair and then never reprice, unlike the CDF/USD makers on the same tick cadence.
mechanism: Unknown. Candidates: reprice threshold expressed in USD-scaled ticks, variance/reservation term collapsing to an unchanged price, or side-state blocked by an unacknowledged request.
falsifier: A full-log run shows ABC/CDF cancel/replace cycles comparable to CDF/USD.

root_cause: Avellaneda-Stoikov risk aversion and fill decay are reciprocal quote-price parameters, but only variance was converted for the CDF-quoted book. The inventory term was therefore k^2=9e6 too small (8.3e-6 CDF against a 1e-3 CDF tick), so the cross-pair maker could never move a tick and behaved as a static quoter.
fix: stoikovConfigScaled converts variance by 1/k^2 and both reciprocal parameters by k, making the control law quote-scale invariant.

claim: The multi-venue market has no price anchor: the only price setters estimate their own volatility from a midpoint they themselves set, so the quote diverges superexponentially after roughly 11 simulated minutes.
mechanism: A price move raises the maker's variance estimate, which widens the Avellaneda-Stoikov risk term, which moves the reservation price and the quote further, which produces a larger observed move. Noise traders take random sides and hold no view, so nothing opposes the drift.
partial_fix: Relative (log-return) variance with dimensionless risk parameters removed the price-level dependence and made the control scale invariant, delaying onset from 657s to 673s. It does not break the feedback loop.
next: Add an exogenous fundamental value process and a value-trading participant, so the anchor comes from flow that opposes deviation rather than from maker configuration. This directly answers the FFA question of which components are necessary for a market to persist.
falsifier: A 20-minute run of research/ffa-ecology-control-2026-08-15.json keeps every ABC/USD book two-sided and within a bounded band of its bootstrap price.

claim: Implied volatility inverted from traded option prices is strongly tenor dependent even though the dealer quotes a single flat 80% IV, because its spread is a fixed fraction of the underlying rather than of vega.
mechanism: OptionMarketMaker sets half-spread = spotMid * SpreadBps/10000 = 150 USD at a 50,000 USD underlying, independent of tenor. A 6h option premium is roughly 416 USD and a 48h premium roughly 1,200 USD, so the same absolute spread is ~36% of the short-dated premium and ~12% of the longer one.
impact: Any volatility-surface, skew, or vega experiment measures the dealer's spread convention, not a volatility process. A vega-proportional or vol-space quoting mode is required before surface claims.
note: The convention is documented in the dealer config, so this is a modelling limitation rather than a defect.

claim: Dated futures have makers but no takers, so no carry or term structure forms.
mechanism: Noise flow is configured only for ABC/USD and ABC-PERP, and no carry arbitrageur exists, so dated-future books receive quotes and no trades.
note: Mark-based term structure is flat by construction because the engine marks a dated future at the underlying index; only traded prices can show carry.

resolution: Three changes together: an exogenous fundamental value process, informed value traders that cross the visible book against it, and a maker volatility estimate taken from trade prints with a cap instead of from the maker's own quoted midpoint.
result: Runs that previously diverged at 657-673 simulated seconds now complete at 20 minutes, 90 minutes and 4 hours with the mid oscillating around the 50,000 anchor.
residual: See FFA-10: anchoring capacity is finite.

claim: Price anchoring is capacity limited: when informed inventory saturates, the quoted price detaches from fundamental value and only returns once informed capacity is restored.
mechanism: Each value trader is bounded by MaxInventory and by its funded balance, so a sustained maker-driven drift can exhaust the informed side. With no informed flow opposing it the price wanders until inventory or the deviation reverses.
why_it_matters: This is the FFA question in miniature: which participants are necessary, and how much of them. The excursion size should scale with informed capital and edge threshold, which is a directly testable prediction.

claim: The maker control depends on risk aversion and inventory horizon only through their product, and the configured value sat where the variance cap bound the spread.
mechanism: The reservation shift and the risk component of the spread are both gamma*sigma^2*tau, so gamma and tau are not separately identified. At the configured product of 3 the risk term exceeded any plausible spread and the cap set the quote.
impact: Every pre-calibration magnitude, including E-055, describes a market whose spread was set by a parameter cap rather than by risk.

claim: The perpetual has no anchoring mechanism: it can sit at its funding cap, several hundred basis points from spot, for tens of minutes.
mechanism: Informed participants trade only the spot book, and the scenario has no spot-perp basis arbitrageur. Funding is the only restoring force, it is capped, and the cap is reached well before the basis closes.
observation: In a calibrated 90-minute run the north perpetual basis fell to -300bps at minute 50, stayed pinned there with funding at its -75bps cap until minute 76, then recovered.
next: Add a basis arbitrageur with an executable, fee-aware, fill-reconciled ledger, then measure whether the funding cap or the arbitrageur's capital is the binding constraint.

claim: A medium-frequency informed trader is competitively excluded, not merely disadvantaged, by a fast informed trader running the identical strategy.
mechanism: Both act on the same deviation from fundamental value. The faster participant re-evaluates 300x more often and reaches the venue 100x sooner, so every opportunity is consumed before the slower participant's next evaluation.
falsifier: A latency distribution with a heavy tail, or a passive-posting medium-frequency rule, gives the slow tier non-zero fills and non-zero marginal effect on price efficiency.

claim: Reaction cadence, not transport latency, determines whether an informed strategy is profitable in this market.
mechanism: An informed participant only acts on deviations it has observed. Evaluation cadence bounds how many deviations it can see at all, while transport latency only shifts when its order arrives relative to a deviation it has already identified.
note: Slower transport was mildly better for a lone informed participant: it left larger deviations standing and collected them, since it faced no competing informed flow.
falsifier: Two informed participants at identical cadence but different transport latency should show the transport axis mattering; that race has not been run.

claim: The simulation step bounds the latency an experiment can resolve.
mechanism: Scheduled deliveries within one advance are indistinguishable, so a latency below one step produces results identical to zero latency.
rule: An experiment quoting a latency must set the engine step below it and report both. A treatment smaller than the step looks exactly like a null result.

claim: The simulated market does not reproduce the Wyart-Bouchaud spread-volatility relation: spread is a configured parameter rather than a price for adverse selection.
mechanism: At the calibrated risk aversion the volatility-dependent term of the Avellaneda-Stoikov spread, gamma*sigma^2*tau, is negligible against the constant fill-decay term (2/gamma)*log1p(gamma/kappa). The makers therefore quote a fixed fraction of price.
consequence: Any result that depends on spreads widening with volatility or with informed-flow intensity is currently invalid.
next: Make market makers marginally profitable so the spread is derived from realised adverse selection; this test is the acceptance criterion.

claim: MDPublisher.Subscribe replaced a client's feed list for a symbol instead of adding to it, so a strategy asking for a second feed silently lost the first.
mechanism: Subscriptions are keyed by (symbol, client) and Unsubscribe removes a whole symbol, so there was no way to hold two feeds. A market maker asking for snapshots and then trades kept only trades.
impact: Introduced when makers began estimating volatility from trade prints. Their forward froze at the bootstrap price, which made the market artificially stable and their quotes insensitive to conditions. The calibration in E-057 and the spread-volatility falsification in E-066 were both measured in that state and must be re-run.
fix: Subscribe now merges feed types for an existing (symbol, client) subscription; regression in tests/marketdata_test.go.

claim: With a working forward feed the stable band of maker risk aversion is far lower and narrow.
mechanism: A live forward lets a price move re-enter the quote, restoring the feedback the frozen forward had masked. Above about 1e-4 the market diverges within 30 simulated minutes; below about 2e-6 the spread reaches the tick floor and further reduction changes nothing.
note: The window between divergence and the tick floor is where inventory can influence quotes at all. At the chosen value inventory skew is far below one tick, so makers are effectively fixed-spread quoters, which is the same limitation FFA-16 identified.

claim: Metaorder impact grows sublinearly with executed size.
caveat: One seed, one decade of size, no participation-rate control arm. The discriminating test is whether the exponent is independent of participation rate, which has not been run.
next: Widen the size range, sweep participation rate at fixed size, and bootstrap over seeds.

note: Re-run after the market-data subscription fix. The conclusion and its stated mechanism both survive: spread is 41.1 ticks in nearly every cell regardless of noise intensity, fundamental volatility or informed-trader count, and only the maker's own risk aversion moves it.
analytic_check: The measured relative spread of 0.0082% matches the fill-decay term (2/gamma_rel)*log1p(gamma_rel/kappa_rel) = 0.0080% at the calibrated parameters, confirming the volatility-dependent term contributes almost nothing.

claim: A participation-rate control is meaningless unless it is measured against volume traded by other participants and the minimum child size is small enough not to bind.
mechanism: The trade feed includes the agent's own fills. Pacing against total volume is self-feeding, and the realised rate approaches one by construction once the agent is a large share of trading. Separately, a minimum child size floors the child quantity, so in a thin market the floor sets the pace rather than the rate.
note: The intermediate value of 2.698 is the honest measurement: pacing was corrected but the child floor still bound, so the agent traded 2.7 times everyone else. Only lowering the floor and adding external volume brought the realised rate to its configured value.

claim: After the subscription fix the market is stable for about two simulated hours, not six.
note: A six-hour run fails terminal valuation with or without metaorder traders, so this is the base market rather than the execution agent. Impact measurement needs long stable runs, so this bounds the experiment.
next: Either extend the stable horizon or run impact experiments in two-hour blocks and pool across seeds.

claim: The market has no anchor for its market makers, so the quoted price is a self-referential multiplicative random walk that wanders arbitrarily far from fundamental value once informed capacity saturates. FFA-07 was never closed; it was masked by the frozen forward.
mechanism: Makers take their forward from their own book midpoint and quote symmetrically around it, so the mid reproduces itself. Their inventory term is far too small to pull the quote back: at the calibrated risk aversion an inventory of 100 ABC shifts the quote by 0.6 basis points. Value traders lean against the deviation until they reach their inventory bound and then stop, after which nothing opposes the walk.
ruled_out: Rounding asymmetry: replacing floor-bid/ceil-ask with nearest-tick rounding reproduced the same trajectory.
Volatility feedback: the estimate sat at 1e-9, two orders below its cap, until after the divergence had already begun.
The execution agent: the same failure occurs with metaorder traders removed.
Informed capacity alone: raising the inventory bound and adding informed participants made every seed fail sooner.
next: Makers need a reference that is not their own midpoint. The options are an exogenous index, a cross-venue consensus price, or an inventory term large enough to matter, and each is a different market model rather than a parameter change.

claim: A cross-venue consensus reference stabilises a market that cannot stabilise itself, even though the consensus contains no information the venues do not already have.
mechanism: Each venue's makers quote around the median of the venues' midpoints instead of their own. A single venue drifting cannot move the median, so it is pulled back by the other two. Collective drift remains possible in principle but requires a majority to move together.
note: The stabilising ingredient is aggregation across independent price setters, not exogenous information.

claim: Anchoring makers directly to the true fundamental value is worse than anchoring them to a consensus of their own midpoints: the idealised anchor fails while the endogenous one survives.
mechanism: With makers pinned to value the price cannot drift, and in this population price drift is the only channel through which makers shed inventory: they have no working inventory control. Their positions therefore accumulate monotonically until one side of a book can no longer be quoted.

quantities.failure: terminal valuation on venue central: ABC/USD no longer two-sided

implication: Price drift is doing the work that an inventory term should do. Fixing FFA-16 is a prerequisite for the idealised anchor to be viable, which makes the two findings one problem seen from two sides.

claim: Anchoring price to value and bounding maker inventory are in tension in this population: no configuration achieves both over twenty-four hours.
mechanism: Maker inventory is the mirror image of everyone else's net position, so it can only return to zero if some participant unwinds. Value traders unwind only when the price crosses fair value, so pinning the price to value removes the very excursions that would let makers flatten. Skewing quotes to shed inventory instead moves the midpoints the consensus index is built from, so the skew contaminates its own anchor.
implication: Bounded maker inventory needs flow that mean-reverts in quantity, not only in price. That is a missing participant rather than a parameter: something must take the other side over long horizons.
next: Add a participant whose demand mean-reverts in quantity, then re-test the matrix.

claim: Market-maker inventory is the mirror of whichever participant accumulates, and removing one accumulator only reveals the next.
mechanism: Random-side noise flow mean-reverts in price but not in quantity, so its net position is a random walk that makers must hold the other side of. Replacing it with round-trip participants removes that channel entirely, but then informed traders become the accumulator: they take the side of the fundamental's cumulative drift and, unlike a round trip, never unwind while the drift continues.
note: In seed 92 the informed traders sit exactly at their aggregate cap of 1200 units, and the makers hold 1205 against it. The identity is close to exact because these are the only participants carrying directional risk.
implication: Bounding maker inventory needs a participant that supplies the asset as value rises rather than merely trading round trips. Until then, maker inventory tracks the fundamental's cumulative drift.
non_replication: A single seed suggested round-trip flow bounded maker inventory at 24h (mean 16.4, max 41.0 with 0.02% mispricing). Seeds 92 and 93 did not reproduce it (6% mispricing, inventory near 190), so that claim is withdrawn.

claim: Neither a price-elastic supplier nor an exit rule for informed traders bounds market-maker inventory. Maker inventory is the mirror of whichever participant's net position random-walks, and every population tried so far contains one.

why_each_failed.elastic_supplier: Its target keys off a fixed reference price, and under an anchor that holds the price near a random-walking fundamental the target oscillates around zero. It adds two-way flow without absorbing a drift, and maker inventory rose slightly rather than falling.
why_each_failed.informed_exit: With noise flow present the informed traders are already flat, at 0.2 to 0.6 units net, so an exit rule has nothing to unwind. It matters only in the population where they are the marginal directional participant.

conclusion: Maker inventory growth is generic to being the counterparty of random-walking demand. The only thing that bounded it in any experiment was maker-side inventory skew, which FFA-25 showed conflicts with an endogenous anchor. That tension is a property of this market design rather than a parameter to tune.

claim: Market orders with immediate-or-cancel sent by the spot makers to the perpetual book are accepted, never fill, and produce no cancellation, while the same book trades normally for every other participant.
ruled_out: Book empty: the perpetual is two-sided in 99.9% of snapshots and trades 3,561 times in the same run.
In-flight flag stuck: rejections and cancellations now clear it.
Self-cancellation by the maker: the maker no longer cancels acknowledgements for its own hedge requests, and the behaviour is unchanged.
note: Hedge quantity is about one base unit and constant across attempts, while the maker's own inventory reaches 25 units, so the quantity the maker computes and the exposure it carries also disagree.
next: Trace one hedge order through admission and matching. Until it is resolved, maker hedging cannot be evaluated and stays off by default.

sharpened_claim: A marketable order from the spot maker to the perpetual book is accepted and never matches, even when its limit price is 5.2% through the visible touch.
decisive_measurement: Hedge buy at 5,022,990,000 against a book ask of 4,997,140,000, repeated across attempts; 1,218 attempts and 0 fills in thirty simulated minutes while the book was two-sided in 1,438 of 1,442 observations.
ruled_out_now: Engine cannot fill perpetual market IOC: an isolated exchange test fills both within and beyond displayed depth.
Empty hedge book at decision time: the maker now subscribes to it and observes it two-sided 99.7% of the time.
Stale pricing: pricing 50bps through the touch changed nothing, and the measured order price is already 5.2% through it.
Oversized order: the hedge is now capped at the visible size at the touch.
Self-cancellation and stuck in-flight flags: both fixed earlier and instrumented.
next: Reproduce inside the multivenue package with a forced hedge and assert a fill, then bisect between the isolated exchange test and the scenario. The difference is the scenario's deterministic ingress and phase runtime.

cleared: The deterministic phase runtime carries crossing orders correctly. A minimal reproduction inside the same runtime — one actor resting a perpetual ask, another crossing it through the touch — fills exactly as expected. Every earlier taker result measured under this runtime is therefore unaffected.
remaining: In the full scenario the maker's hedges are accepted, do not fill, do not rest, and produce no cancellation. The perpetual book holds a steady 0.2 units a side throughout, so the orders are not resting; only 4 of 13,708 attempts produced a position update.
next: Grow the minimal reproduction toward the scenario one element at a time — spot book, borrowed inventory, several actors, index anchor — until it breaks. Log archaeology has reached its limit here.

root_cause: The hedge price was not aligned to the hedge instrument's tick, so the venue rejected every order with INVALID_PRICE. Pricing through the touch is what knocked it off the grid: a 50 basis point bump on a 50,000 price is 250, which is not a multiple of the 1,000,000-unit tick.
why_it_took_so_long: A rejection is not a fill, and nothing in the scenario summary distinguished the two. The maker retried every tick, so the only visible symptom was inventory that never came down. The exchange log line that looked like an acceptance belonged to a different order.
how_it_was_found: Growing the passing minimal reproduction toward the scenario until it broke, then counting rejections rather than reading logs. The minimal harness had passed only because its prices happened to land on the tick grid after the bump.
fix: Round the hedge outward to the hedge tick, up for a buy and down for a sell, so the order stays marketable after alignment.

claim: Hedging into a second instrument reduces the risk a market maker carries without degrading price accuracy, unlike skewing its quotes.
mechanism: A hedge moves delta to another book instead of moving the maker's own quotes, so it does not disturb the midpoints that price discovery and the consensus anchor are built from.
caveat: Two seeds, and the reduction is partial because each hedge is capped at the visible depth of the perpetual, which is a fifth of a unit against a one-unit band. It also relocates risk to the perpetual maker rather than removing it from the system.
next: Replicate across more seeds and measure where the hedged delta ends up.

replication: Five seeds, twelve simulated hours each, fundamental anchor. Mean net delta falls in every seed and peak net delta falls in every seed, with deviation from value unchanged at 0.0002.

claim: Hedging does not remove risk from the population, it concentrates it in whoever does not hedge.
mechanism: A hedge is a trade, so the delta a market maker sheds is acquired by its counterparty. With only the spot makers hedging, the perpetual maker ends up holding both the noise flow's perpetual position and the spot makers' hedges.
note: The spot makers offset roughly half of their short by buying perpetuals, and the perpetual maker's resulting position is larger than any single spot maker's. Partial hedging is a capacity limit: each hedge is capped at the perpetual's visible depth.
implication: A population needs a participant that is delta neutral by construction and carries the basis instead, which is what a cash-and-carry arbitrageur is. Otherwise hedging only relocates the accumulation problem.

claim: The population has no delta-neutral sink for directional risk, and the reason traces back to market makers not pricing inventory.
chain: Makers do not price inventory into their quotes: an eightfold change in volatility moves the spread by one percent, and only the configured risk aversion moves it (FFA-16).
Both the spot and the perpetual maker therefore quote the same function of the same published index, so their midpoints coincide to the unit and the basis is identically zero.

A cash-and-carry participant needs a basis to trade. Measured: two arbitrageurs per venue placed zero orders over twelve hours at entry thresholds of 20, 10, 3 and 1 basis points, and the run output was byte-identical across all four.
With no delta-neutral participant, directional risk has nowhere to settle. Hedging only moves it to whoever does not hedge (FFA-30).
implication: Inventory-sensitive quoting is not a refinement here. It is the precondition for a basis, for carry participation, and for risk to be absorbed rather than relocated.
next: Make the inventory term bind without contaminating the anchor. FFA-25 showed skew conflicts with an endogenous consensus anchor; under the exogenous anchor that conflict may not arise, which is the experiment to run.

refinement: The conflict between inventory skew and price accuracy is a property of the endogenous consensus anchor, not of skew itself. Under the exogenous anchor a 25 basis point skew costs almost nothing: mean deviation from value is 0.0009 to 0.0013 across three seeds, against 3.67 under the consensus anchor at the same skew.
reason: A consensus built from the venues' own midpoints moves when the skew moves those midpoints, so the skew contaminates its own reference. An exogenous reference cannot be moved by the quotes that key off it.

claim: Inventory-sensitive quoting is the precondition for a basis, and a basis is the precondition for delta-neutral participation. Turning it on produces both.
note: The carry participant's two legs offset to within a hundredth of a unit, so it is delta neutral as designed.

limits.absorption_is_small: With carry participants the perpetual maker's position moves only from -1188.1 to -1176.0 units while the carry pair holds 24.8 against -24.2, so the concentration identified in FFA-30 is barely relieved.
limits.risk_reduction_is_seed_dependent: Maker net delta improves from 41.8 to 32.8 on one seed and is unchanged on two others.
limits.upper_bound: A 100 basis point skew fails outright.

next: Raise the carry participant's capacity and measure whether absorption scales with it, which separates a capacity limit from a structural one.

claim: How much risk a delta-neutral participant can absorb is bounded by displayed quote size, not by its own capital.
mechanism: An immediate-or-cancel taker cannot lift more than is displayed at the touch, so a carry participant's throughput is set by the makers' quote size however much capital, position limit, or lot size it is given.
note: A fourfold increase in participants and a fiftyfold increase in lot size raised absorption by less than a third and then saturated exactly, while a twenty-fivefold increase in displayed size raised it twentyfold.
resolution: This closes the arc that began with market makers accumulating without bound. The population can bound maker inventory: with five-unit quotes the spot makers run at 2.7 to 3.7 units of net delta against 32 to 55 with fifth-unit quotes, the carry participants hold about 650 units in offsetting legs, and deviation from value is at its best measured value of 0.0002.

claim: The simulated market reproduces long-memory order flow together with diffusive prices, which is the empirical tension Bouchaud et al describe.
note: The decay is slow across three decades of lag while the variance ratio stays within five percent of one. The lag-one correlation of 0.019 is far below the lag-two value of 0.329 and needs explaining separately; a genuine long-memory series should not dip at the first lag.
caveat: Order flow is 65% sells over this run, so the sign series is not balanced and the autocorrelation is measured around a non-zero mean.

claim: The configuration that makes the market accurate also removes price impact: the measured response to a trade is indistinguishable from zero.
mechanism: Makers quote deep size around an exogenous reference they cannot influence, so a trade is absorbed without moving the price. Accuracy is bought by making the price exogenous, and impact is exactly what an exogenous price cannot have.
implication: The anchor choice decides which regularity the simulator can reproduce. An exogenous anchor gives accuracy, stability and bounded inventory but no impact; an endogenous one gives impact and drift. The square-root impact law cannot be tested on this baseline, and the earlier metaorder measurements were made before it existed.
next: Measure impact as a function of anchor weight: blending the index with the book midpoint should trade accuracy against impact continuously, and the point where a square-root law appears is the interesting one.

claim: Price impact and price accuracy trade off continuously along the maker's anchor weight, and there is a middle range where both are acceptable.
mechanism: The anchor weight sets how much of a maker's reference it can influence. At full weight the reference is purely exogenous, so trades are absorbed without moving price. As the book midpoint enters the reference, a trade moves the midpoint, which moves the next quote, and impact appears.
note: At weights of 0.7 and 0.3 the response rises with lag and then flattens, which is the shape the transient-impact picture predicts, while deviation from value stays under ten basis points and maker inventory stays near three units.
significance: This is the first configuration in the campaign where the market is accurate, stable, risk-bounded and has measurable impact at the same time, so it is the one on which the impact literature can be tested.

claim: Metaorder impact in this market is superlinear in size, not square root.
note: The exponent depends on which bins are fitted because the smallest bins straddle zero, but every fit is well above one, so the sublinear concavity the literature reports is absent.
likely_cause: Impact here is mechanical: a parent order depletes a quote of fixed displayed size that refreshes on a timer, and the maker's reference includes the midpoint it just moved. Neither mechanism produces the concavity that a vanishing latent supply near the price does.
next: The literature attributes the square root to liquidity that vanishes linearly near the transaction price. Testing that here needs a latent-liquidity participant, not a parameter change.

claim: Impact cannot be measured against a fundamental that moves as much as the impact does.
rule: Reduce exogenous price noise, or raise the sample far enough that it averages out, before reading an impact curve. A sample of 29 to 325 metaorders against a drifting fundamental produced sign-alternating nonsense that looked like a measurement.

claim: Adding a latent-liquidity population does not produce the square-root impact law in this market.
interpretation: With a deep displayed book the exponent falls from the 1.24-2.07 range to 1.35 but stays superlinear, and thinning the displayed book removes measurable impact altogether while tripling the trade count and degrading price accuracy fortyfold.
why_it_probably_fails: The theory requires the metaorder to consume a latent density that vanishes linearly at the transaction price. Here the metaorder still trades against displayed maker quotes, and the latent participants act as extra reactive flow rather than as the liquidity being consumed. Their reservation prices are also deposited uniformly in a band, which need not produce the V shape the derivation depends on.
next: Measure the latent density directly before measuring impact again: reconstruct the average volume required to move the price by a given distance and check whether it grows linearly with that distance. Without that shape the exponent cannot be expected to follow, and a market whose displayed book is a thin veneer over latent liquidity, with no continuously quoting maker, is the configuration the derivation actually describes.

claim: The market's supply curve has the shape the square-root law is derived from: the volume needed to move the price by x grows as x squared.
method: First passage, independent of metaorders: from each trade, walk forward accumulating signed volume until the midpoint has moved by at least x, and take the median consumed volume.
note: A square-root law requires an exponent of two here; linear impact would require one.

correction: The superlinear exponent of 1.24 to 2.07 was measured with metaorders of about one unit, while moving the price by a single basis point takes roughly forty-five units in this market. Those metaorders were one to two orders of magnitude too small to register, so the fit described background noise rather than impact.
conclusion: With parent orders spanning six to sixty-seven units the impact exponent is 0.52 to 0.61 across three seeds, consistent with the independent supply-curve measurement of 0.482 and with the reported one half.
caveats: About 250 metaorders per seed, the smallest size bin is noise dominated and negative on two seeds, and the fit is over four bins spanning about one decade.

claim: The square-root impact law in this market is produced by mean-reverting quoting against a reference, not by latent liquidity. The exponent is therefore not diagnostic of the mechanism the literature attributes it to.
mechanism: A maker that quotes around a reference it cannot move applies a restoring force proportional to the displacement of the price from that reference. The volume needed to hold the price x away then grows as x squared, which inverts to square-root impact. Stiffness changes the prefactor rather than the exponent, which is what the anchor-weight sweep shows: the exponent stays near two while the volume needed per basis point moves.
consequence: Latent participants change the level of liquidity, lowering the volume needed to move one basis point from 65 to 45 units, but leave the exponent unchanged. Reproducing the exponent is therefore weak evidence for the latent-liquidity picture; the discriminating tests are the conditional ones, such as independence from participation rate and the predicted scaling of the prefactor with deposit and cancellation rates.

claim: The latent-liquidity prefactor prediction fails here: the volume needed to move the price does not scale with the deposit rate.
expected: Denser latent liquidity should require more volume to move the price, so the volume per basis point should rise with the deposit rate.
observed: It is non-monotone when intentions cross, and falls fourfold when they rest, while the exponent stays near two throughout.
implementation_gap: An intention here only expresses itself once its reservation price has already crossed the market, so it arrives as demand rather than as supply. Making it rest instead does not change that, because a price that has crossed the touch is marketable anyway. A faithful emulation has to reveal intentions as resting liquidity while they are still near but not through the price, so the visible book approximates the latent density the derivation integrates over.
status_note: The exponent near two is unaffected by any of this, which is consistent with FFA-41: it comes from the makers, not from this population.

claim: Revealing latent intentions as resting liquidity closes the modelling gap but does not change the result: the supply-curve exponent stays near two and the latent population never makes the price harder to move.
conclusion: Across every configuration tried — absent, crossing, resting after crossing, and revealed near the price — the exponent sits between 1.78 and 2.39 while the volume needed per basis point varies by a factor of seven. The exponent is a property of the makers and the prefactor is a property of everything else, which is the cleanest statement this campaign has produced about where the square-root law comes from here.
cost: Revealed intentions are expensive: an hour of simulated time with two participants holding up to three hundred intentions each took two minutes fifteen of wall time, against seconds without them, because each reveal and pull is an order.

claim: The strong form of the square-root law cannot be tested in this market, because participation rate is not a controllable treatment.
reason: Each child order is capped at the depth displayed at the touch, so realised participation is set by the makers' quote size rather than by the configured rate. Sweeping the rate tenfold left realised participation between 0.017 and 0.024 in every cell, so the treatment never applied.
what_would_be_needed: Either execution that can walk multiple levels rather than stopping at the touch, or displayed depth scaled alongside the rate so the cap does not bind. Until then any statement about independence from participation rate would be about a parameter with no effect.

claim: At this sample size the metaorder-binning estimator of the impact exponent is unusable, while the supply-curve estimator is stable.
note: Roughly 340 metaorders spanning less than one decade of size give exponents from 0.32 to 1.54 across seeds and nominal treatments, a spread twelve times wider than the supply-curve estimator measured on the same market.
consequence: This retro-qualifies the earlier agreement at 0.609, 0.518 and 0.553: three values that close together were partly fortunate, and the supply curve at 0.482 was carrying the result. Impact-exponent claims here should be made with the supply curve, with metaorders used only as a consistency check.

fix: Two caps had to be removed before participation was a treatment at all. A child order was capped at the size displayed at the best price, so it could never take more than the makers showed; and the minimum child size dominated the rate whenever it exceeded the rate times recent volume.
result: With a slippage allowance letting a child walk levels and a small child floor, realised participation now tracks the configured rate: medians of 0.0010, 0.0047 and 0.0091 for configured rates of 0.05, 0.20 and 0.50, monotone across a tenfold range.
remaining_blocker: Statistical resolution rather than mechanism. The metaorder-binned exponent varies by 1.22 across seeds at roughly 340 metaorders, while the effect being tested is whether the exponent shifts at all, so the arms cannot be separated. Each arm now yields only 150 to 235 metaorders, which is worse.
what_would_be_needed: Either far more metaorders per arm, or an estimator with the stability of the supply curve applied per arm. The supply curve measures the market rather than the parent order, so it cannot be conditioned on participation without a redesign.

claim: In the full population the strategies with a stable positive result are the ones that do not carry direction, and the market makers on the main pair lose consistently.
reading: Option dealers and carry arbitrageurs earn a tight, repeatable result: 722,000 and 183,000 US dollars with spreads of about 20,000 and 25,000 across seeds. Option flow and spot makers lose just as repeatably. Everything whose result depends on the direction it happened to be holding — noise flow, elastic suppliers, informed traders — swings sign between seeds, in one case by six million.
note: The active result subtracts the participant's own initial holdings valued at terminal marks, so it removes revaluation of starting inventory but not the directional outcome of positions acquired during the run. That is why the delta-neutral classes are the stable ones: they end flat, so nothing is left to be lucky about.
next: A hierarchy inside one mixture is not yet a non-transitive structure. Testing that needs the same classes measured across different opponent mixtures to see whether the ranking reverses.

claim: Dominance between market making and carry arbitrage reverses with the measurement horizon, in the same population with the same seed.
mechanism: A carry participant pays the spread to establish two legs and only earns as the basis converges and funding accrues, so its result starts negative and turns positive with time. A market maker collects the spread immediately and pays for it later through inventory and adverse selection. The two curves cross.
significance: This is the first genuinely non-transitive structure the campaign has found, though it is non-transitivity in horizon rather than in opponent space: there is no horizon-free answer to which of the two strategies is better, and any ranking must state the horizon it was measured over.
caveat: Two seeds and one opponent mixture. The opponent-space matrix run alongside it showed carry negative in all four mixtures at three hours, which is consistent with the horizon effect dominating composition at that length.

claim: There is no rock-paper-scissors structure in opponent space in this ecology. The ranking is a strict hierarchy and no strategy's sign reverses against any opponent mixture.
reading: Carry arbitrage dominates execution, which dominates informed trading, in every column. What does vary is magnitude: every strategy earns least against the carry-heavy mixture, so carry participants are the ones competing for the same mispricing everyone else is paid for.

claim: Returns to carry arbitrage are strongly negatively frequency dependent: the per-participant result falls roughly as the inverse of density while the total extracted barely grows.
reading: A twelvefold increase in carry participants cuts each one's result nearly eightfold while the pool they share grows by only about half, so the basis behaves as a nearly fixed resource. The market makers pay for it: their loss per member deepens from 44,000 to 72,000 US dollars as carry density rises.
significance: Negative frequency dependence of this strength is what allows strategies to coexist at some proportion rather than one taking over, so this ecology is stabilised by congestion rather than by a non-transitive cycle. Per-member returns are still positive at the highest density tested, so the carrying capacity lies beyond twenty-four participants per venue.

correction: The totals reported earlier were wrong by a factor of three. Participant counts are per venue and there are three venues, so the totals were computed against the per-venue count rather than the number of participants. The per-member figures were correct and the conclusion is unchanged.

claim: Total extraction by carry arbitrage is hump shaped in density: it rises to a maximum and then collapses, so the ecology has an optimum population and an overcrowded regime beyond it.

quantities.peak_near: 96 participants per venue, 288 in total, at about 341,000 US dollars over twelve simulated hours

reading: Per-member returns fall roughly as the inverse of density throughout, but the pool itself grows only until about 96 participants per venue and then shrinks by nearly forty percent at 192. Beyond the peak the participants are no longer sharing a resource, they are degrading it: they trade against each other and pay fees on both sides before the basis they are chasing has time to converge.
market_maker_side: Maker losses do not deepen past the peak either, moving between 62,000 and 72,000 US dollars per member across the whole range, so the extra crowding is not being funded by the makers. It is dissipated.
significance: This gives the campaign a quantitative carrying capacity, which is what the rock-paper-scissors question was really after: not who beats whom, but how many of a strategy this market can support before the strategy destroys its own edge.

claim: The cross-asset markets were never anchored: the venue published an index only for the main pair and the perpetual, so the CDF and cross makers fell back to their own midpoint and diverged.
how_it_surfaced: Raising the market-maker count to eight per venue produced participant results in the tens of billions on about thirty billion of starting capital: 74.4 billion for the cross-pair makers against minus 67.3 billion for noise flow.
fix: The index is now published for every quoted market, keyed by symbol, with the fundamental converted into each contract's units, and it is seeded before the first quote rather than at the first automation tick.
verification: The same run gives the cross-pair makers minus 56,791 US dollars, and the figures for the main pair are unchanged: option dealers 232,782 per member against 232,786 before, spot makers minus 7,660 against minus 7,551.
invalidates: Every abc_cdf_spot_maker figure reported in FFA-46, FFA-48 and FFA-49, including the 140,431 per member that made it the campaign's apparent best strategy. Those were an unanchored book drifting, not an edge. Conclusions about carry arbitrage, market making, option dealing and option flow rest on the main pair and are unaffected.

claim: Market making has no profitable density in this configuration: it loses at every count tested, and adding makers reduces the loss per participant while increasing it in total.
reading: Spreading the same adverse selection across more makers dilutes what each one loses without changing the fact that the class pays. This is the opposite shape to carry arbitrage, whose per-member return falls with density from a profitable level, and it means the two strategies have different carrying-capacity structures rather than a common one.
caveat: Measured with no carry participants present and with makers anchored to an exogenous reference, which removes the excursions they would otherwise earn from.

changes: The cross-pair makers move from the campaign's apparent best strategy to a consistent loser, and noise flow becomes positive on all three seeds rather than swinging by six million. Both were consequences of the unanchored cross book draining into the cross makers.
unchanged: The stable winners and losers are the same and their magnitudes barely move: option dealers around 240,000 per member, carry arbitrage around 31,000, option flow around minus 105,000, spot makers around minus 50,000. The claim that delta-neutral classes earn repeatably while directional classes are dominated by path luck survives, with the perpetual maker as the clearest directional example, ranging from minus 104,000 to minus 1.3 million.

claim: The perpetual trades persistently rich by about 86 basis points, and this is the source of both the carry participants' edge and the perpetual maker's losses.
reading: The premium is present in 99.5% of paired observations and tightly distributed between 80 and 86 basis points, so it is a standing feature rather than an excursion. Carry participants collect it as funding, and the perpetual maker receives funding too yet still loses, because it carries the directional position that absorbing this flow requires.

claim: The persistent premium is not caused by the funding cap. Raising the cap more than fivefold leaves it and the losses it causes essentially unchanged.
prediction: With funding saturating at 75 basis points against a basis of 86, raising the cap should let funding close the gap, shrinking the premium and the carry edge with it.
reading: Carry returns rose by a fifth and the perpetual maker's loss fell by under two percent, which is the opposite of what a funding-limited premium would do. Something other than funding sets the level.
remaining_candidates: The perpetual maker's own inventory skew, since absorbing a persistently one-sided flow moves its reservation price away from the index in exactly this direction.
A difference between the mark used for funding and the midpoint the basis is measured against.
next: Measure the perpetual maker's net position and its quoted reservation against the published index over a run. If the premium tracks its inventory, the premium is the price of the risk it is being asked to hold rather than a funding artifact.

claim: The perpetual's standing premium is the maker's inventory skew divided by its index weight. Partial anchoring amplifies a skew by the reciprocal of the weight.
derivation: The maker quotes a skew s away from a reference that blends the index with its own midpoint, r = w*index + (1-w)*mid, and its midpoint is that reference plus the skew. At the fixed point mid - index = s / w.
reading: The maker is persistently short by about 180 to 310 units because it absorbs one-sided derivative flow, and it prices that risk with a skew. Anchoring only partly to the index multiplies the resulting displacement, so the observed premium of 83 basis points is a 25 basis point risk price amplified 3.3 times by the feedback of its own midpoint.
explains: Why raising the funding cap did nothing (FFA-54): the premium is set by the maker's quoting, not by funding. It also identifies what carry participants are really paid for, which is the maker's inventory risk rather than a funding inefficiency.
caveat: Inventory sits far beyond the maker's configured risk limit, so the skew is clamped at its maximum throughout; the law is verified in that saturated regime.

test_of_the_caveat: The law was previously verified only where inventory exceeded the risk limit and the skew was clamped. Raising the limit fivefold drops the maker to 30% of its budget: inventory moves from 177.5 to 149.9 units short against a limit of 500, so the skew falls from its maximum of 25 basis points to 7.5, and the premium falls from 83.4 to 24.1 basis points against 25.0 predicted.
reading: Both factors are now verified independently. The anchor weight sets the amplification and the inventory fraction sets what is amplified, so the premium a market charges for absorbing one-sided flow is the product of how much risk its maker carries relative to its budget and how loosely that maker is tethered to an outside reference.

claim: The perpetual maker's risk limit reorganises the whole payoff table: it nearly eliminates carry arbitrage's edge and moves more than a million dollars of losses from the perpetual maker onto the spot makers.
mechanism_established: A larger risk budget means the maker prices a given position with less skew, so the premium falls: 83.4 basis points at a limit of 100 against 24.1 at 500. Carry participants are paid that premium, so their edge falls with it, and the perpetual maker stops paying the price of its own aggressive quoting.
unexplained: The collapse in carry's result is far steeper than the premium's. The premium falls by a factor of 3.5 while carry's result falls by a factor of 90, and the entry threshold of 2 basis points is too low to explain it. Spot makers also deteriorate sevenfold, which the premium alone does not account for.
next: Record carry trade counts, holding times and realised entry basis across the same sweep. If trades collapse rather than margins, the strategy is being starved of qualifying opportunities; if margins collapse, the cost of crossing is eating a smaller premium.

answer: Carry's collapse is a margin collapse, not a shortage of opportunities. Raising the maker risk limit from 100 to 200 units leaves the participants trading more, not less — fills rise from 1,104 to 1,738 and volume from 1,904 to 3,028 units — while the median basis they enter on falls from 85.81 basis points to 0.27.
why: The risk limit is shared by every market maker, so raising it shrinks the skew on the spot book and the perpetual book together. What carry participants trade is the difference between those two books, and that difference collapses even though the perpetual's premium against the index only falls from 83.4 to 24.1 basis points.
distinction_worth_keeping: The perpetual's premium against the index and the basis a carry participant can actually trade are different quantities. The first is what the premium law describes; the second is what pays the strategy, and it depends on how much both makers skew rather than on the perpetual maker alone.

claim: Spot market makers lose money because carry arbitrage extracts from them. Removing carry's edge, by loosening only the perpetual maker's risk budget, turns spot making profitable.
reading: With only the perpetual maker's budget changed, the basis carry can trade falls by a third and its result falls by a factor of twelve, while the spot makers move from losing 61,805 US dollars per member to earning 2,850. The perpetual maker's own result is unchanged at about minus 1.3 million.
consequence: The campaign's earlier finding that market making is unprofitable at every density is conditional. It holds while carry arbitrage is profitable, because the two are the same transfer seen from both ends. It is not a property of market making itself.

claim: Carry profitability is convex in the tradable basis, consistent with a fixed round-trip cost that consumes most of a thinner basis.

quantities.implied_breakeven_basis_bps: roughly 50, from taker fees of 5 basis points on each of four legs plus the cost of crossing two spreads

note: A 1.48-fold reduction in the basis entered on produces a 12.66-fold reduction in result, so the strategy is earning the excess over a fixed cost rather than the basis itself. The break-even estimate is arithmetic, not measured.
next: Measure realised cost per round trip directly from the carry participants' fills and fees, and check whether result tracks basis minus that cost.

what_was_predicted: A fixed round-trip cost of roughly 50 basis points, from fees and spread crossing, consuming most of a thinner basis.
what_was_measured: Fees are exactly 5.00 basis points of notional at both settings, one taker fee per fill. The cost is an order of magnitude below the estimate and cannot explain a twelvefold change in result from a 1.5-fold change in basis.

claim: Carry arbitrage earns funding and loses on execution and marks. Its result is the difference, which is why a modest fall in the premium nearly eliminates it.
reading: Funding income falls by a quarter while the result falls by ninety-two percent, because the non-funding side of the strategy deteriorates at the same time, from minus 12,821 to minus 30,436 per member. The strategy trades slightly more notional for a thinner premium and pays for it twice.
significance: Carry arbitrage here is not an arbitrage. It is a funding carry financed by a persistent execution loss, and it is profitable only while the funding rate is high enough to cover that loss. That is why it collapses when the perpetual maker's skew, which sets the funding rate, is reduced.

prediction: If the result is funding income minus a persistent execution loss, then suppressing funding should leave carry with exactly that loss, while its basis and activity stay unchanged.
accuracy: The implied non-funding result from the earlier decomposition was minus 12,821 per member; suppressing funding gives minus 12,746, a difference of 0.6 percent. The basis entered on and the number of fills are identical, so only the funding channel was removed.
conclusion: Carry arbitrage in this ecology is a funding carry. Without funding it is a loss-making strategy that trades exactly as much and at exactly the same prices.

original_mechanism: Stated as a gradual effect: carry pays the spread to establish two legs and earns as the basis converges and funding accrues, so the two strategies' curves cross somewhere between six and twelve hours.
measured_mechanism: The reversal is a discrete funding settlement. Funding is paid once every eight hours, and the ranking flips across that payment: carry earns minus 13,216 US dollars per member at seven hours and plus 34,144 at nine, while the spot makers go from plus 17,405 to minus 45,082.
control: With funding suppressed the three-hour results are identical to the funded run, because no payment has occurred yet, and the twelve-hour reversal disappears entirely: carry earns minus 12,383 and the makers plus 12,742.
what_survives: Dominance really does depend on the horizon, and no ranking in this campaign is meaningful without one. What is corrected is the reason: the crossover is set by the venue's funding interval rather than by an emergent convergence timescale, so it would move if the interval did.
consistency_check: Carry's result at seven hours, minus 13,216, matches the pure execution loss of minus 12,746 measured by suppressing funding, as it should before any funding has been paid.

claim: The horizon at which carry arbitrage overtakes market making is set by the venue's funding interval, and moves when the interval moves.
reading: Halving the funding interval halves the crossover horizon: the ranking flips between seven and nine hours at the default and between three and five hours at four. The three-hour results are identical under both intervals, since no payment has occurred either way.
significance: This makes the campaign's non-transitivity result a statement about venue design rather than about strategies. Which of two strategies looks dominant is a choice the venue makes when it sets its settlement frequency, and an evaluation window shorter than that interval systematically favours the market maker.

test: Order-flow persistence was attributed in the literature to order splitting, so the execution agents were removed and then every strategic participant, leaving only market makers and independent noise takers.
finding: Persistence is highest with makers and independent noise alone, so splitting is not its source here. Noise takers draw their side independently, but their orders only execute where liquidity happens to be, and inventory-skewed makers supply it asymmetrically. Independent intentions are converted into persistent realised signs by the availability of liquidity.
corrected_claim: The statistic is reproduced; the mechanism is not. This is the same distinction as the square-root exponent, which is produced here by maker mean reversion rather than by latent liquidity.
supporting_anomaly: Buy fractions are 0.398, 0.278 and 0.325 across the three populations, all strongly sell-skewed, which is consistent with liquidity being available asymmetrically rather than with balanced flow.

claim: A derivative market with a single dealer is a monopoly rent, and adding competing dealers should compete the rent away rather than simply splitting it.
test: Option dealer and futures maker counts were made configurable, then run at one dealer per venue, three dealers per venue with flow held fixed, and three dealers per venue with flow tripled.
result: Supported. With flow fixed, per-dealer result falls 83 percent and the class total falls 49 percent, while each option taker's loss falls 47 percent. The refinement is that dealer income is a function of the flow-to-dealer ratio alone; restoring that ratio by tripling the flow restores per-dealer income to its monopoly level (236,175 against 231,543).
caveat: The dated futures ladder remains inert across all arms, so this is many-vs-many in options only. Making the futures ladder alive needs a participant class that takes dated futures risk, which does not yet exist.

claim: The dated futures ladder is inert because it has no term structure, not because it lacks a counterparty population.
test: Wired the existing CashCarryArb and ParityArb classes into the multivenue population, then compared spot-pinned against self-anchored dated quoting.
result: Supported. With the futures mid pinned to spot the basis is identically zero and the carry desk never trades at any edge. Self-anchoring the dated books gives the futures maker 12,799 USD per member against -0.94 when pinned.

claim: Spot market orders from the dated carry desk are accepted by the exchange and then never fill.
test: Full event logs for the two central-venue carry desks over 12h.
result: 104 spot market orders OrderAccepted, zero OrderFill and zero OrderRejected, while the same actor's futures market orders filled 156 times. The central spot book traded 179,871 times over the same window, so the book was not empty. Consequence: the delta-neutral carry strategy silently degrades into a naked short futures position.
next: Root-cause the market-order admission path; the failure is venue-specific in this run, so compare the price_time and pro_rata venues.

result: Not an admission bug and not a strategy calibration problem. Quote replacement empties the book once per step, and deterministic phase ordering puts specific actors inside that hole every step.

claim: The maker-vs-maker volume concentration and the taker fill failures are the same artifact: cancel-then-replace quoting leaves the book empty at a deterministic instant in every step.
test: Reconstruct the book from the delta stream and count steps containing an empty side.
result: 99.5 percent of 41,751 steps contain an instant with both sides empty, matching the 99.5 percent maker-vs-maker volume share measured separately.
prediction: Replacing quotes without emptying the book (submit before cancel, or amend in place) should collapse maker-vs-maker volume share and raise taker fill rates together. If only one moves, they are not the same cause.
next: Implement submit-before-cancel in the spot maker and re-measure both quantities.

context: FFA-58 claimed the maker-vs-maker volume concentration and the taker fill failures are the same artifact of cancel-then-replace quoting.
arm_b: unchanged cancel-first makers plus a passive BootstrapDepth ladder that rests 10 levels a side at 5 bps spacing and never reprices, refilling only what is consumed.

predictions_registered_before_running.arm_a_if_same_artifact: empty-step fraction falls toward zero AND maker volume share falls, together.
predictions_registered_before_running.arm_b_if_depth_availability_binds: dated carry desk spot fill rate rises well above its 11.2% baseline.
predictions_registered_before_running.arm_b_if_not: fill rate stays near 11.2% despite a book that is essentially never empty, which would point away from the phase-hole explanation entirely.

caveat_registered: Arm B cannot hold the empty-step fraction high, because a permanently resting ladder necessarily lowers it. Its discriminating power is in the fill rate, not in the emptiness measure.
partial_result_arm_a: From a run interrupted at 8.4h of 12h: empty-step fraction (both sides) 99.5% -> 1.9% on central, but maker volume share only 97.8% -> 95.0%, while total filled quantity nearly doubled and absolute non-maker volume rose about fourfold. On the registered criterion this weakens the same-artifact claim: the hole collapsed and the concentration did not follow.
status_note: Full 12h reruns of both arms in flight; partial figures to be replaced by complete ones.

claim: Non-maker classes across the whole ecology fail to execute, and at least two separable mechanisms are involved: the book being empty at the acting instant, and the submission price being stale relative to the book at match time.
discriminating_test: Order style is the lever. If emptiness alone binds, market and IOC orders fail at equal rates. Measured 44.9 percent against 0.008 to 11.2 percent, so emptiness alone is insufficient.
open_question: Whether the IOC failures are stale prices, tick misalignment, or a phase position that differs per actor. Instrumenting rejection reasons and match-time top of book per submitted order would separate these.
consequence_if_true: Every payoff comparison in this campaign needs re-reading, since execution ability confounds strategy quality.

result: Atomic replacement collapsed the empty-step fraction from 99.5 to 1.9 percent and repaired fill rates across every class, while maker volume share moved only 97.9 -> 95.0 percent. The two are not the same artifact.
Arm A resolved: hole collapses, execution repaired, concentration persists. Arm B (bootstrap ladder) still running.

The claim that two separable mechanisms were needed is refuted for execution: emptiness alone accounted for it. The claim that campaign payoff tables are confounded by execution ability is strongly supported, with five classes flipping sign between regimes.

claim: Spot maker volume concentration has a cause other than the intra-step liquidity hole.
note: Persisted at 95.0 percent after the hole was removed and every other class began filling normally. Candidate mechanisms: makers crossing each other during the overlap window that atomic replacement creates, quote sizes far larger than taker demand, or both makers anchoring to the same index and therefore quoting into each other.

claim: Silent config-field mismatches can make an experimental arm indistinguishable from its control.
result: Confirmed and closed by construction. Strict decoding now rejects unknown fields, and the audit found two archived configs whose snapshot interval never bound.
campaign_note: Two runs in this campaign were invalidated by stale binaries or ignored fields. Any arm whose result exactly equals its control should be treated as a tooling failure until proven otherwise.

result: Not a behavioural pathology. By trade count maker-versus-maker is 9.5 percent under cancel-first and 19.8 percent under atomic replacement, against 89.8 to 95.4 percent of volume. The concentration is dominated by a quote-size to taker-lot-size mismatch, on top of a real but minority crossing rate.

claim: The residual maker-versus-maker crossing rate is driven by inventory-skew divergence between two makers anchored to the same index.
prediction: Setting maker_inventory_skew_bps to zero should cut the crossing rate by count; leaving skew on but giving the makers different index weights should raise it.
falsifier: If the crossing rate is unchanged with zero skew, the cause is the shared anchor or the quoting cadence rather than skew divergence.

result: Both arms complete. Arm A (atomic replacement) repairs execution across every class. Arm B (passive ladder) repairs market-order takers only, while eliminating book emptiness entirely. The arms separate two failure modes that a single remedy would have conflated.

The original claim that two separable mechanisms are at work is supported after all, though not as first stated. It is not market versus IOC order style per se, but depth existing versus depth existing at the taker's limit price. The intermediate retraction in E-129 was itself wrong.

claim: A passive ladder that never reprices is profitable in this ecology because it quotes a fixed band around the exogenous fundamental.
prediction: Its profit should fall as fundamental_log_vol_per_step rises, and should invert once per-step fundamental moves routinely exceed its 5 bps band.
note: If it stays profitable at high fundamental volatility, the profit comes from the taker fee structure or from the band width rather than from information.

result: Dealer income tracks the flow-to-dealer ratio and competition transfers rent to the flow; both hold within about one percent after the execution fix.
Execution ability confounds spot-side taker payoffs, not the whole campaign. The derivative arms replicate unchanged.
Zero inventory skew cuts maker-versus-maker crossings from 19.8 to 5.6 percent of trades, confirming skew divergence as the driver.
The ladder's profit rises with fundamental volatility instead of falling, by a factor of 121 across a twentyfold volatility increase. It is the informed side rather than the adversely selected one.

claim: The published index is a zero-lag, noise-free channel to the exogenous fundamental, so any actor that quotes directly on it holds perfect information and dominates as volatility rises.
prediction: Adding lag or observation noise to the index feed should collapse the ladder's edge, and should compress the volatility scaling from 121 times toward flat.
falsifier: If the ladder stays profitable under a lagged and noisy index, its edge comes from the band width or the fee structure rather than from information.
significance: This is a modelling decision with ecology-wide consequences. Strategies are currently ranked partly by whether they consume the index directly, and the makers deliberately handicap themselves by blending it at weight 0.3.

claim: The maker population has a volatility carrying capacity: above some fundamental volatility, market making is not viable at any of the configured parameters.
note: At twenty times baseline volatility every maker class loses and every taker class profits. This is the kind of regime change Bouchaud's non-equilibrium framing predicts, and it is worth mapping as a boundary rather than treating either side as the normal case.

result: A lagged, noisy index does not collapse the ladder's edge; at low volatility it improves it. The test cannot separate the ladder's information advantage from everyone else's because the degradation was global.
next: Degrade only one subscriber's view, or remove the ladder's structural advantage first.

claim: The never-repricing ladder is profitable because it is the only continuously resting depth, not because it observes the fundamental without lag.
prediction: Against makers that also quote continuously (submit before cancel), the ladder's advantage should fall sharply at both volatilities.
falsifier: If the ladder stays comparably profitable against continuously-quoting makers, presence is not the source and the informational reading returns.
